strengths: Novel combination of Bayesian cross-validation with data fission for single-measurement model selection in imaging, with sound theoretical connections to marginal likelihood and posterior predictive checks
Addresses a genuine and important problem: model evaluation without ground truth is critical for scientific imaging where multiple independent measurements are infeasible
Broad applicability to modern imaging pipelines with deep learning-based priors, multiple sampling schemes (Langevin, diffusion), and various noise models (Gaussian, Poisson)
Solid mathematical development with careful derivations, proper Monte Carlo approximations, and thorough analytical treatment of the Gaussian case including error analysis
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple applications (deblurring, MRI) with appropriate statistical testing (Type I error, power analysis) and extensive supplementary details
Well-designed scoring rules addressing different aspects: likelihood-based for likelihood evaluation, posterior-based with embeddings for OOD detection in ill-posed problems
Honest and appropriate limitations discussion without overclaiming, acknowledging convergence issues, failure modes at extreme parameters, and embedding dependence
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons—only compares against single Bayesian residuals method (2021); no comparison with recent alternative model selection approaches, making relative merit assessment difficult

Ad-hoc and unprincipled α selection with no guidance for new applications; different experiments use different values (0.5 vs 0.25), undermining practical applicability and creating a hyperparameter tuning burden

Moderate experimental success rates (86.7% single-shot accuracy, 60% on MRI knee scans, 80% OOD detection) with meaningful failure modes (e.g., Figure 8 showing method fails for high-blur OOD detection)
Heavy dependence on embedding choice for posterior-based rule (LPIPS vs Dinov2) requiring domain expertise, with no principled guidance for embedding selection and no automated framework provided
Slow Monte Carlo convergence in Gaussian case (Figure 11) with incomplete resolution; while Appendix C argues fine convergence unnecessary, Figure 16 demonstrates cases where this matters
Insufficient computational cost analysis—claims of 'low computational cost' lack quantitative support; no detailed timing comparisons or scaling analysis provided
Limited experimental diversity focusing primarily on deblurring and MRI; broader application domains (CT, photoacoustic imaging, microscopy) would strengthen generality claims

Theoretical analysis gaps including limited bias analysis of measurement splitting versus true posterior predictive check, absence of finite-sample convergence rates, and no guidance on selecting K and N hyperparameters
Method assumes high-quality posterior sampling from p(x|y⁻); error propagation for difficult posteriors (multimodal, ill-conditioned) not thoroughly analyzed
Code availability not directly verifiable (URLs redacted in manuscript); reproducibility depends on availability of specific pre-trained diffusion models
